# Stock exchange (securities market) (`stock_exchange`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by joint_stock_company, public_debt_bonds, newspapers_periodicals
- Core idea: A fixed place and hours where shares and bonds are bought and sold among many traders through brokers, with standard settlement days and published prices. Its value is liquidity: an investor buys a share in a 20-year venture because he knows he can sell it next week, so companies and states can raise long-term money cheaply, and the price summarises what traders collectively expect. Minimum design: transferable securities with a register of owners, licensed brokers bound by rules, a fixed settlement procedure, and printed price lists.
- Pitfalls:
  - Taking the market price for the true value: prices swing with fear and fashion
  - Allowing purchases on borrowed money without limits: a fall forces sales and becomes a crash (1720, 1929)
  - No disclosure rules: insiders and promoters pump and dump
  - Banning short sales or futures: Amsterdam tried in 1610 and trading simply continued informally
- History: europe: 13th–14th c. – Venetian and Genoese public debt claims change hands; 15th c. merchants meet at the van der Beurse inn in Bruges; 1531 Antwerp Bourse building; 1602–1611 VOC shares traded in Amsterdam, Beurs opened 1611, with forwards and options; 1688 de la Vega describes it; 1698 Castaing's price lists in London; 1801 London Stock Exchange; east_asia: 1697–1730 – Dojima rice market in Osaka, officially licensed 1730, trades standard rice futures; 1878 Tokyo Stock Exchange; americas: 1792 – Buttonwood Agreement founds the New York brokers' exchange; india: 1875 – Native Share and Stock Brokers' Association, Bombay; islamic: 1866 – Istanbul securities exchange (Dersaadet Tahvilat Borsası); china: 1891 – Shanghai Sharebrokers' Association
- Read:
  - Joseph de la Vega, Confusión de confusiones (1688)
  - Larry Neal, The Rise of Financial Capitalism (1990)
  - Edward Chancellor, Devil Take the Hindmost: A History of Financial Speculation (1999)
